messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Firefighter
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

James is a 34-year-old firefighter who has been married for six years. He sought help eight months after returning from a three-month deployment as a relief worker in a conflict zone, a role he had volunteered for through his department’s international aid program. The trauma that now governs his waking life occurred on his third week there. He and a small team were evacuating civilians from a village that had come under shelling. As they loaded a bus, a mortar round struck a building twenty feet away. James was knocked to the ground, and when he stood up, he saw that a young mother and her child, who had been running toward the bus, were no longer standing. He remembers the silence that followed the blast, the way the dust settled, and the feeling of his own hands shaking as he tried to lift debris. He did not sleep for the next three days. He kept working. When he finally returned home, he told himself he was fine—that he had seen worse, that he was trained for this.

But within weeks of being back, James began to notice a persistent tension that had not been there before. At the firehouse, he found himself checking the location of every exit the moment he walked into a room—the bay, the kitchen, the bunkroom. He would note the nearest door, the windows, the path to the stairwell, and he would position himself so that he could see all of them at once. He did this without thinking, and he did it everywhere: at the grocery store, at his son’s school play, at the diner where he and his wife used to go for breakfast on Sundays. He had come to believe that danger could arrive without warning, and that the only way to stay safe was to know exactly how to leave. His wife noticed that he no longer sat with his back to the door at restaurants. When she asked him about it, he said he was just being careful.

At home, the vigilance did not stop. James felt on guard even inside his own house. He would wake in the middle of the night, heart pounding, listening for sounds that were not there. He found himself scanning the front yard through the blinds before stepping outside to get the mail. He began to feel threatened by strangers approaching him in ordinary situations—a neighbor walking over to borrow a tool, a delivery driver at the door, a man asking for directions at a gas station. He knew, intellectually, that these were not threats. But his body did not believe it. His chest would tighten, his jaw would clench, and he would feel a surge of adrenaline that made him want to move, to get away, to find cover.

To manage this constant state of alert, James developed a set of habits that he initially thought of as reasonable precautions. He made sure to stay close to an exit in any enclosed space, and he avoided exercise—not because he was out of shape, but because he had learned that the physical sensations of exertion, the elevated heart rate and shortness of breath, felt too much like the moments after the blast. He could not separate the feeling of a good workout from the feeling of terror, so he simply stopped running and lifting weights. He also began to push away positive emotions when they arose. A moment of laughter with his wife, a sense of pride when his son scored a goal in soccer—these feelings felt unsafe, as if letting his guard down for even a second would invite disaster. He had come to believe that feeling good was a kind of vulnerability, and that the only way to stay prepared was to stay flat.

The consequences of these strategies accumulated slowly. His wife told him he seemed distant, that he was not really present. She did not know about the scanning, the vigilance, the way he pushed her hand away when she reached for him in bed. At work, his captain noticed that James had become quieter, more withdrawn. He no longer joined the other firefighters for pickup basketball on their days off. He had stopped going to the gym entirely, which was unusual for him. His physical fitness, once a source of pride and a job requirement, had become a casualty of his survival instincts.

What finally brought James to seek help was a moment in the firehouse kitchen. A new recruit walked in behind him without making noise, and James spun around, his hand going to his hip where his radio was clipped, his breath coming fast. The recruit stepped back, startled. James apologized, but he could not stop shaking. That night, he told his wife that he needed to talk to someone. He is afraid of what is happening to him—afraid that he is becoming someone his family does not recognize, and afraid that if he lets himself feel the full weight of what he saw, he will not be able to function at all. But he is also, quietly, hoping that talking about it might help him find a way back to the person he used to be.
